title: What Is a Hagwon? Inside Korea's After-School Cram School Culture
html:
In many Korean neighborhoods, entire buildings are filled with small schools that open after the regular school day ends. Each one is a hagwon (학원), and together they form one of the most expensive habits of Korean family life.

In one line

A hagwon is a for-profit private academy where Korean students take extra classes, most often after school, in subjects from math and English to piano and coding.

Where the word comes from

Hagwon is written 學院 in Chinese characters: hak (學) means "learning" and won (院) means "institution" or "hall." English writers usually translate it as "cram school," although many hagwons teach sports, art or music rather than exam prep.

A short history

Private tutoring has long been a point of conflict in Korea. In 1980 the military government of Chun Doo-hwan banned private tutoring to ease the pressure on families. The Constitutional Court struck that ban down in 2000, and the private education market grew rapidly after that.

Cities have also tried to limit hours. In 2009 Seoul and Busan set a 10 p.m. curfew for hagwon classes, and the Constitutional Court upheld the limit that year.

How much do families spend?

A lot. Wikipedia, citing 2022 government data reported by CNN, says Koreans spent about 26 trillion won (around 19 billion dollars) on private education that year. The Korea Times reported in 2025 that a lawmaker's office put the 2025 figure at 32.5 trillion won, and that a 2024 Ministry of Education survey found nearly half of preschool-age children attending some form of private class.

In the news

The cost keeps driving policy debates. In July 2025 a bill was proposed to restrict cram-school instruction for very young children. In September 2026 an education researcher proposed in Kyunghyang Shinmun renting empty public-school classrooms to academies in the evening to bring fees down, while admitting that current rules forbid for-profit use of schools.

Don't confuse it with

  • Gwaoe (과외): one-to-one or small-group private tutoring, usually at home.
  • An "English kindergarten": a hagwon for preschoolers taught in English, not a real kindergarten under the law.
  • After-school programs (방과후학교): cheaper classes run by public schools themselves.
